opus-5.5.text:
I think the interaction will be quite different from what we're used to with chatbots today. Right now, most people interact with AI the way they'd use a search engine or a very smart assistant: you type something, it answers, and you go back and forth. That's synchronous. You sit there and wait.

With agents, I think a lot of the interaction becomes asynchronous. You give an agent a task, maybe something that takes hours or days, like researching a topic, writing and testing a piece of software, or handling some workflow for you. Then you go do something else, and it comes back with results, or it comes back with questions when it actually needs your judgment. It's more like working with a colleague or delegating to a team than chatting with a tool.

So the key questions shift. It's less "how good is the answer to this one prompt" and more "how do I specify what I want, how do I trust it, and when should it interrupt me." A lot of the value will come from the interface between human and agent: how context is shared, how preferences are remembered, how the agent knows when to act on its own and when to check in. I think that's actually underexplored. People focus a lot on making the model smarter, but the utility depends just as much on the environment and the interaction design around it.

There's also a spectrum. For some tasks you want a very tight loop, like coding with a copilot where you see every change. For others you want almost full autonomy, where you only see the final outcome. I don't think there will be one form. Different products will find different points on that spectrum, and the interesting innovation will come from people who figure out the right form for a specific kind of work, not just from scaling the model.

Long term, I'd guess the agent becomes something with memory and a persistent relationship with you. It knows your context, your history, your goals, so you don't have to explain everything from scratch each time. That's when it starts to feel less like using software and more like having a partner working alongside you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how agents may work and interact, but does not say they need not take person-like forms.

r002.rationale: It describes agent interaction as more like working with a colleague or partner, and does not propose that it need not resemble interaction with people.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I think about a lot, and honestly my view has shifted over the past few years.

Right now, most people's mental model of interacting with AI is still the chat box. You type something, the model replies, you type again. That's basically the ChatGPT interface, and it's been enormously successful, but I think it's actually a transitional form. It's the interface that made sense when the model could only really do one thing: produce text in response to text.

The thing that changes everything is when the model can act. When I was working on ReAct and later on things like SWE-bench and the agent benchmarks, the core idea was that reasoning and acting should be intertwined. The model thinks, it does something in the world, it observes what happened, it thinks again. Once you have that loop, the interaction with the human doesn't have to be turn by turn anymore. You can give an agent a goal and go away for an hour, or a day, and it comes back with something.

So I think the future looks less like a conversation and more like delegation. You'll describe outcomes, not steps. Today you say "write me a function that does X." In the future you'll say "I want this feature shipped by Friday, here's the context, come back to me if you hit something you can't decide." And the agent will go do the work, including figuring out what questions actually need a human and what it can resolve on its own.

The interesting part is that this makes the human-AI interface a management problem rather than a prompting problem. The skills that matter shift. Being good at prompting is a bit like being good at talking to a very literal intern. Being good at delegating to agents is more like being a good manager: setting the right scope, knowing when to check in, building enough trust to let things run, and also knowing when not to.

I also think the interaction will become much more asynchronous and much more ambient. You won't open an app to "use AI." Agents will be running in the background on your behalf, watching your inbox, your codebase, your calendar, and surfacing things only when they matter. The interface might be a notification, or a short summary in the morning, rather than a chat window you stare at.

There's a catch, which is evaluation. If you delegate, you have to be able to trust the result, and right now that trust is uneven. The agents are great at some things and quietly wrong at others. So a lot of the near-term interaction design is really about verification: how does the agent show its work, how does the human audit it cheaply, how does the system know its own uncertainty. I spent a lot of time on benchmarks precisely because I think you can't build the delegation future without measuring the thing you're delegating to.

And the last thing I'd say is that it will probably feel less like talking to one assistant and more like working with a team. Multiple agents, some specialized, coordinating with each other, with you as the person who sets direction. That's a very different relationship than what we have today, and I think we're only at the very beginning of figuring out what it should feel like.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents running in the background and coordinating, but does not say they need not take person-like forms.

r002.rationale: It says interaction will be less like conversation and more like delegation, with agents working asynchronously and surfacing notifications or summaries instead of requiring a chat window.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll gradually move from telling AI exactly what to do toward explaining what we want to achieve. Today, you often have to break a task into steps yourself: open this tool, find this information, put it into that document. With an agent, you might describe the goal, and it can work out some of those steps for you.

But I don’t think that means people will simply give one instruction and disappear. For many tasks, you don’t fully know what you want until you see an initial result. So the interaction could look more like collaboration: the agent tries something, you give feedback, and together you clarify the goal.

A big question is when the agent should act independently and when it should ask you. If it asks about every little thing, delegating isn’t very useful. If it makes consequential decisions without checking, you may not trust it. I think good agents will need to understand that boundary and make it easy for people to inspect, correct, or stop what they’re doing.

So the interface may become less about individual commands and more about communicating intent, giving feedback, and deciding how much responsibility to delegate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses delegating tasks to agents but says nothing about whether they need person-like forms.

r002.rationale: It describes interaction as collaboration and intent-sharing, but does not state that interaction need not resemble interaction with people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll gradually move from telling AI exactly what to do toward telling it what we want to achieve. Today, you often have to break a task into steps yourself: search for this, read that, compare the results. With an agent, you might describe the goal, give it some constraints, and let it work out the steps.

But I don’t think that means people will simply hand everything over. The interesting question is when the agent should act and when it should come back to you. If it asks about every small decision, you’re still doing all the work. If it never asks, it may spend a lot of time pursuing something you didn’t want. So a good agent needs to understand which decisions it can make independently and which require your judgment.

The interface may also depend on the task. Sometimes conversation is enough. Sometimes you want to see a document, a plan, or the current state of the work and directly change it. I expect interaction to become a combination of conversation and shared work, rather than just a sequence of messages.

Ultimately, I think trust will develop through that process. You give the agent a small task, see how it handles uncertainty and mistakes, and gradually give it more responsibility.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task delegation, agent autonomy, and interfaces, but says nothing about whether agents need person-like forms.

r002.rationale: It describes interaction through conversation and shared work, but does not say that agent interaction need not resemble interaction with people.
